title: Sustained High Windows Process Thread Count
exclusions: This use case reports a Windows Process performance-counter instance whose paired `Thread Count` is greater than 500 in at least three distinct one-minute bins within a closed five-minute window. The 500-thread and three-sample thresholds are local starter policy, not Microsoft limits or proof of “thread exhaustion.” Windows has no universal 65,000-thread ceiling represented by this counter, and a high count alone does not establish a leak, deadlock, .NET ThreadPool starvation, outage, or root cause. The rule does not measure thread state/stacks, per-thread CPU, queue length, request latency, process responsiveness, handle/desktop-heap/commit pressure, total system threads, containers, Linux processes, processes omitted between samples, or instances that cannot be paired reliably with `ID Process`. Classic `Process` instance names are nonunique and can shift when same-named processes start/stop; Windows 11 `Process V2` is preferable where supported, but this cross-version design pairs counters by instance/minute/PID and still requires process telemetry correlation.
evidence: After deployment, retain the expected-host/application/process inventory and owner; Windows builds and Process versus Process V2 support decision; approved 60-second Perfmon input, exact `Thread Count` and `ID Process` counter availability, effective `btool`, forwarder and `Splunk_TA_windows` versions; role/process-specific baseline, 500-thread/three-of-five policy and changes; the `windows_process_sustained_high_thread_count` saved-search definition, ACL, schedule, dispatch history, and triggered-alert records; each result's first/last UTC breach, host, instance, PID, breach sample count, minimum/average/maximum threads, and source metadata; same-time Process Explorer/WPR/WPA or application-profiler evidence, process start/path/command/hash/service/app-pool/container identity, CPU/memory/handles/response time/queue/error/restart data; source-health, instance/PID-pairing, duplicate, and late-data results; bounded exceptions; incident disposition; and dated 500/501, two/three sample, PID-reuse, duplicate-name, recovery, and end-to-end tests. This documentation-only review started no threads/processes, changed no Perfmon input, and created no metric, alert, or production evidence.

controlTest.positiveScenario: In an isolated test index, ingest paired `Perfmon:Process` single-mode rows for `host=win01`, `instance=leaktest`, counters `ID Process=4321` and `Thread Count=501` in each of three distinct one-minute bins inside the closed window. Expect exactly one result with `breach_samples=3`, `min_threads=501`, `max_threads=501`, and PID 4321. Repeat with thread values 501, 550, and 600 and expect min 501, rounded average 550.3, and max 600.
controlTest.negativeScenario: Run isolated variants and expect zero rows for: three samples exactly 500; only two one-minute bins at 501; five healthy bins at 499; `ID Process=0`; `_Total`; Thread Count rows without a paired ID Process in the same minute; ID Process rows without Thread Count; same instance split across PIDs so neither PID has three breaches; a positive set in the newest excluded five minutes; malformed/non-numeric values; wrong counter/object/source type; and duplicate rows confined to only two bins. Verify three breaches for one PID still return one row when another same-named instance/PID stays below threshold.

dataSources: Windows PDH Process performance counters collected locally every 60 seconds by a Splunk `perfmon://` input in single-event mode: `Thread Count` (current active threads in the process) and `ID Process` (PID identity), all instances except `_Total`. The SPL's local convention is `index=perfmon`, `sourcetype=Perfmon:Process`; required fields are `_time`, `host`, `object`, `counter`, `instance`, `Value`, `source`, and `sourcetype`. `useEnglishOnly=true` makes the documented English object/counter names portable. Microsoft documents classic Process names as nonunique and potentially unstable; Windows 11+ Process V2 includes PID in the instance name and should be evaluated separately. A 60-second interval is required for the three-of-five design; Splunk's default is 300 seconds when omitted.
app: Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows (`Splunk_TA_windows`, Splunkbase 742) version 10.0.1 for Perfmon collection, field extraction, and deployment context. A local `windows_process_capacity` app should own the custom Perfmon stanza, saved search, source/pairing health checks, threshold policy, and dashboard. No premium Splunk app is required.
spl:
index=perfmon sourcetype="Perfmon:Process" object="Process" counter IN ("Thread Count","ID Process") earliest=-10m@m latest=-5m@m
| eval host=lower(trim(host)), instance=trim(instance), metric_value=tonumber(Value), thread_sample=if(counter="Thread Count",metric_value,null()), pid_sample=if(counter="ID Process",metric_value,null())
| where len(host)>0 AND len(instance)>0 AND instance!="_Total" AND isnotnull(metric_value)
| bin _time span=1m
| stats max(thread_sample) as thread_count max(pid_sample) as process_id count(eval(counter="Thread Count")) as thread_rows count(eval(counter="ID Process")) as pid_rows by _time host instance source sourcetype
| where isnotnull(thread_count) AND isnotnull(process_id) AND process_id>0 AND thread_count>500
| stats earliest(_time) as first_breach latest(_time) as last_breach count as breach_samples min(thread_count) as min_threads avg(thread_count) as avg_threads max(thread_count) as max_threads sum(thread_rows) as thread_rows sum(pid_rows) as pid_rows by host instance process_id source sourcetype
| where breach_samples>=3
| eval avg_threads=round(avg_threads,1), process_id=tostring(round(process_id,0)), use_case="UC-1.2.57"
| convert ctime(first_breach) ctime(last_breach)
| table first_breach last_breach host instance process_id breach_samples min_threads avg_threads max_threads thread_rows pid_rows source sourcetype use_case
| sort 0 -max_threads -breach_samples host instance
description: Reports one row per host, classic Process instance, and paired PID when Thread Count is above 500 in at least three one-minute bins of the closed five-minute window. The result preserves persistence and minimum/average/maximum count rather than labeling one transient sample as exhaustion.
value: Sustained process thread growth can precede memory/handle pressure, scheduler overhead, slow response, failed work, or a restart even when aggregate CPU appears normal. Pairing Thread Count with PID and requiring persistence reduces transient noise, gives application owners a concrete process to profile, and shortens diagnosis of blocking, runaway concurrency, or role-specific capacity regressions.
implementation: Deploy a local `perfmon://Process_Thread_Identity` input with `object=Process`, `counters=Thread Count; ID Process`, all instances, `interval=60`, `mode=single`, and `useEnglishOnly=true`; validate paired rows and duplicate-name behavior on every supported build. Save the SPL as `windows_process_sustained_high_thread_count`, run every 5 minutes over the delayed closed window, and trigger at three bins above 500. Baseline thresholds by process/host role, correlate PID to process start/service/app telemetry, and implement recovery below policy. Validate boundaries, missing pairs, PID/instance churn, duplicate data, late samples, source silence, profiling workflow, and bounded exceptions.
visualization: Build a process-thread dashboard with expected-host input freshness, pair completeness, and duplicate-instance/PID anomalies first; single values for affected hosts/processes; a line chart of Thread Count by host/instance/PID; a top-process table with persistence and min/avg/max threads; and overlays for CPU, private bytes, handles, application latency/queue/errors, and restarts. Drill down to all Process counters, process creation/service/app-pool identity, Process Explorer thread/stacks, WPR/WPA or runtime profiler evidence, and deployment/change context. Label 500 as the configured threshold—not a Windows limit—and show the active policy version.
schema: Windows PDH Process Thread Count and ID Process samples collected by Splunk Perfmon single mode
dataModelAcceleration: Although `Perfmon:Process` has broad Application State, Performance, and Endpoint mappings in the Windows add-on, no accelerated CIM dataset is claimed to preserve paired per-minute `Thread Count`, `ID Process`, classic instance identity, sample completeness, and three-of-five persistence. A metric-index variant can be designed separately, but it must preserve PID pairing and produce event-for-event threshold parity before replacing this raw search.

knownFalsePositives:
A result is a true sustained count above the configured policy under the collected sample contract; the cause can be normal for a role or temporary workload.

1. **IIS application pool or high-concurrency web workload** — `w3wp` may legitimately run many threads under bursty traffic or blocking dependencies. Resolve app pool/PID, deployment version, request rate/queue/latency/errors, CPU/memory, downstream health, and seven-day role baseline. Tune by exact app pool/host role and SLO—not all `w3wp.exe`.

2. **Java application server, search/index service, or broker** — JVM/native frameworks can create large configured pools. Correlate PID/start arguments, service, JVM/thread dump, pool configuration, workload, GC/CPU/memory, and owner-approved baseline. A count above 500 can be normal but sustained growth beyond baseline remains actionable.

3. **.NET service under short blocking or ThreadPool adjustment** — Microsoft notes ThreadPool starvation is characterized by rising threads with low CPU and supporting queue/work metrics; a high stable total alone is insufficient. Join runtime counters, latency, queue, CPU, thread dump/trace, deployment, and trend before classifying starvation.

4. **SQL Server, backup, antivirus/EDR, management, or monitoring agent** — Privileged agents and databases may use many worker threads during scans/jobs. Match exact process/service/version, job/change ID, expected schedule, workload, configured worker limits, and recovery. Do not exempt the basename across all roles.

5. **Load, resilience, soak, or performance test** — Approved tests intentionally increase concurrency. Require test ID, host/application scope, traffic profile, owner, safeguards, UTC bounds, expected peak/recovery, and post-test baseline. Preserve detector evidence; suppress only duplicate paging.

6. **Process startup/warm-up or deployment overlap** — A new version can briefly create pools while the old process drains. Correlate deployment/change, old/new PID, app-pool recycle, process lifetime, and return below threshold. The three-bin rule reduces but does not eliminate this case.

7. **Classic Process instance/PID rebinding** — Same-named processes can cause `name`, `name#1` identities to shift. Microsoft documents this limitation. Inspect raw paired bins, process start events, Process V2 availability, and PID lifetime. Treat mismatches as telemetry quality, not application failure.

8. **Duplicate Perfmon inputs** — Overlapping local stanzas can duplicate rows. The max per minute should preserve count, but `thread_rows`/`pid_rows` expose duplication. Compare input/source/forwarder deployment and fix collection rather than suppress the host.

**Safe suppression:** preserve raw samples and base result. Apply notification exceptions after detection through a reviewed lookup keyed to exact host role, application/service identity, instance plus validated executable/PID context, threshold/persistence policy, deployment/job/test ID, owner, approver, and exclusive epoch bounds. Reject basename-only, all-Java/IIS/SQL, host-wide permanent, wildcard, or broad maintenance exclusions; never suppress source/pairing loss, PID/instance ambiguity, monotonic growth, failed recovery, breached application SLO, unknown process, or simultaneous memory/handle/CPU/error pressure.
reviewer: documentation-only editorial review against Microsoft Process ThreadCount/IDProcess, classic duplicate-instance/Process V2, .NET starvation, and Process Explorer troubleshooting documentation plus Splunk Perfmon input, interval, source-type, CIM, and Microsoft Windows add-on documentation; counters, input, pairing, fixtures, threshold, process load, profiling, alert delivery, exceptions, recovery, and production response were specified but not executed or Microsoft/Windows performance/Splunk/application SME-signed

cost.search_load_notes: A 60-second all-process input emits two counter rows per process per minute, materially more than Splunk's 300-second default. The search bins and pairs five minutes of data. Measure process count, events/bytes, forwarder CPU, lag, duplicate rows, and scheduler memory; use role-scoped deployment or validated metrics design at scale.

detailedImplementation:
## Prerequisites and threshold contract

Assign Windows performance, application/service, runtime (.NET/JVM where relevant), Splunk collection/content, telemetry-health, and incident owners. Inventory every monitored host, Windows build, Process/Process V2 availability, host/application role, expected process/service/app-pool identities, normal PID/thread-count range and growth, CPU/memory/handle/queue/latency SLOs, maintenance authority, and retirement state. A process name alone is not identity.

Microsoft defines Thread Count as the number of threads currently active in a process. It is a raw current count, not a percentage, rate, queue, pool availability metric, or operating-system limit. Remove the former assertion that Windows has a roughly 65K system-wide thread ceiling. Resource limits depend on architecture, address space, commit, stack size, desktop heap, quotas, and workload. This UC only says “above local policy persistently.”

The starter policy is `thread_count > 500` in at least 3 distinct one-minute bins of one closed 5-minute window. Exactly 500 and only two breach bins are negative. Change the value only after role baselining, capacity review, fixture updates, runbook impact, and versioned approval. For .NET ThreadPool starvation, Microsoft recommends interpreting rising ThreadPool threads alongside low CPU, queue/work metrics, and response impact; generic Process Thread Count cannot make that diagnosis.

## Step 1 — Configure paired Perfmon sampling

Deploy `Splunk_TA_windows` from Splunkbase 742. Put a custom stanza in `windows_process_capacity/local/inputs.conf`, not the add-on default:

```ini
[perfmon://Process_Thread_Identity]
object = Process
counters = Thread Count; ID Process
instances = *
interval = 60
mode = single
useEnglishOnly = true
index = perfmon
disabled = 0
```

Splunk documents `interval` in seconds and a 300-second default when omitted; explicitly use 60 seconds for three-of-five. `mode=single` is part of this event contract because each counter is a row with `counter` and `Value`. Verify the installed version's exact casing (`useEnglishOnly`) and effective configuration with `splunk btool inputs list --debug`. The `index=perfmon` name is local. Avoid a duplicate default/custom Process stanza.

On canaries, compare Splunk samples with Perfmon/PowerShell for `\Process(*)\Thread Count` and `\Process(*)\ID Process`. Confirm `object=Process`, English counter strings, `instance`, numeric Value, host/source/source type, interval, and timestamp. Verify `_Total` and PID 0 exclusion. Check same-named processes and start/stop churn.

Microsoft documents classic Process instance names as EXE-based, nonunique, and liable to confusing `name#1` matching glitches. Windows 11+ Process V2 includes PID and should be preferred for a separate supported design, but do not change the object name in this SPL without field/fixture validation. Changing the `ProcessNameFormat` registry can break consumers and is not an automatic remediation. This design pairs Thread Count and ID Process in the same host/instance/minute and later groups by PID; it reduces but cannot eliminate classic-instance ambiguity.

Create health searches for expected host with no Perfmon:Process in 5 minutes, missing one counter, pairing ratio below policy, more than one distinct PID per instance/bin, duplicate counter rows, nonnumeric/negative values, sample interval drift, future time, lag over 5 minutes, input process errors, and unknown source type. Route pairing defects to telemetry health.

## Step 2 — Create and understand the saved search

Save as `windows_process_sustained_high_thread_count`; run every 5 minutes. At 12:15, `earliest=-10m@m latest=-5m@m` selects 12:05–12:10 and allows 5 minutes for collection/forwarding. Measure p95/p99 lag and move both bounds together. Trigger when result count is positive; key cases to `host,instance,process_id` and require a later healthy paired sample for recovery.

The base clause scans only the two counters from Process in the exact local index/source type. `tonumber` rejects malformed samples. The first `where` requires host/instance/value and removes `_Total`. One-minute `bin` aligns paired counters. `stats max` produces one Thread Count/PID per bin and exposes duplicate-row counts; if multiple conflicting values exist, health checks must investigate rather than relying silently on max.

The next filter requires a paired positive PID and count above 500. Final `stats` groups by PID so an instance that rebinds to another process does not combine breaches. `breach_samples>=3` establishes persistence. Minimum, average, and maximum show severity/trend. With irregular collection, three bins can span less/more than expected; source-health validates the 60-second cadence.

No CIM/tstats alternative is claimed. Broad Performance/Endpoint mappings do not guarantee exact paired counters and persistence. If a metrics index is adopted, design dimensions for host, object, instance, PID, and counter; prove 500/501 and two/three-bin parity with this search before migration.

## Step 3 — Validate pairing, persistence, and real behavior

Run the exact fixtures and assert columns/values. Test 499/500/501, two/three/five bins, missing/multiple pairs, duplicate rows, PID zero, `_Total`, null/nonnumeric/negative, out-of-order arrival, earliest/latest boundaries, and delayed samples. Test same instance switching PID and same-named parallel processes. Confirm no PID accumulates three breaches unless its own paired bins qualify.

Perform an approved nonproduction load test with application owners; do not create thousands of threads on production. Use a test process/runtime harness with bounded maximum, timeout, memory guard, and cleanup. Capture baseline, raise above 500 for three samples, verify Perfmon/result/alert, then return below threshold and verify recovery. Separately test a short transient above 500 that spans at most two bins and expects no alert.

For IIS/Java/.NET/SQL or the relevant runtime, compare the generic Process count to application/runtime counters, request queue/latency, CPU, private bytes, handles, GC, errors, and restart behavior. Use Process Explorer Threads/Stack, Windows Performance Recorder/Analyzer, dump, `dotnet-counters`, thread dump, or vendor profiler under approved diagnostic procedure. Count identifies a candidate; stacks/traces identify blocking/runaway cause.

Measure events/bytes per host, `splunk-perfmon.exe` CPU/memory, input errors, pair completeness, duplicate rows, lag, search runtime/memory, result count, and owner response. Record Windows/forwarder/TA/Splunk/app versions, input hash, fixtures/test ID, exact UTC bounds, expected/actual rows, search SID, alert/case, and recovery. Keep `draft` until human owners sign off.

## Step 4 — Triage and response

When a result fires: (1) verify three raw paired bins and stable PID/instance; (2) map PID to current/historical executable, path, command, service/app pool/container, start time, hash/signature, and owner; (3) inspect trend before/after the window and process restarts; (4) compare CPU, memory/commit/private bytes, handles, system total threads, queues, latency, errors, and workload; (5) inspect runtime pools and thread states/stacks with approved tooling; (6) correlate deployment/configuration/dependency incidents; and (7) assess user impact and redundancy.

Escalate faster for monotonic growth, breached latency/availability SLO, rising memory/handles/commit, queue growth, repeated crashes/recycles, critical service, multiple affected hosts after a deployment, or no owner/baseline. A high stable count with healthy SLO can be lower urgency but still needs baseline review.

Do not automatically kill/restart the process, recycle an app pool, change runtime thread-pool limits, alter stack size, reboot, or take a full dump from this threshold alone. Restarts can hide the leak and dumps can contain secrets. Follow service-owner diagnostic/change runbooks, preserve evidence, and coordinate failover. Recovery requires later paired below-policy samples and restored application health—not missing data.

## Step 5 — Troubleshoot collection and interpretation

- **No samples:** check local Perfmon counters, counter names/localization, `useEnglishOnly`, input stanza, `splunk-perfmon.exe`, service account, `btool`, output queues, index/source type, and time.
- **One counter missing:** verify both names in the same stanza and single mode; inspect Windows counter availability and parser. Do not estimate PID from instance suffix.
- **Instance maps to changing PIDs:** classic Process limitation. Inspect raw bins/start events, consider validated Process V2 on supported hosts, and route ambiguity to data quality.
- **Rows duplicate:** inspect overlapping stanzas/deployment apps/forwarders. `thread_rows`/`pid_rows` expose duplicates; fix the input.
- **Only one sample per five minutes:** interval defaulted to 300 or config did not deploy. Three-of-five cannot work; alert collection health.
- **Thread count differs from Task Manager/Process Explorer:** align exact time/PID, sampling delay, process lifetime, permissions, and counter source. Fast-changing values naturally differ.
- **High count but no incident:** compare role baseline and SLO/runtime evidence. Tune exact role/process policy after review, not a global executable exception.
- **App is slow below 500:** threshold is not comprehensive. Investigate queue/thread states/dependencies/CPU/memory; role threshold may be lower or different metrics needed.
- **Alert remains after restart:** inspect closed-window bounds, late events, PID grouping, duplicate data, and recovery query. Do not stretch the active search over stale history.
- **Metric-index migration differs:** validate dimensions, one-minute bins, PID pairing, null handling, and exact boundaries against raw fixtures before cutover.
grandmaExplanation: A busy program uses threads to do work. If one Windows process keeps more than 500 threads active for several minutes, we point the application team to that exact process so they can check for blocked or runaway work before users are affected.
hardware: Supported Windows client/server systems exposing Process `Thread Count` and `ID Process` counters to a local Splunk forwarder. Evaluate Process V2 on Windows 11+; classic Process remains necessary for older cross-version deployments and has documented duplicate-name limitations.
